title: Explicit Row Locking: FOR UPDATE & FOR SHARE
description: Prevent lost updates with SELECT FOR UPDATE, implement high-concurrency job queues with SKIP LOCKED, and handle deadlocks.

data.text: When building concurrent workflows (such as reservation booking or background job dispatching), multiple transactions reading the same row can cause **lost updates**. PostgreSQL provides explicit row-level locking via **`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`**.
Building High-Throughput Job Queues with `SKIP LOCKED`

In standard locking, worker processes wait on locked rows. Using **`SKIP LOCKED`**, workers skip already-locked rows and grab the next available unlocked job, providing linear scale without lock contention!

data.title: Concurrent Background Worker Job Claiming
data.content: Multiple worker nodes can execute this simultaneously without blocking each other.

data.text: `SELECT FOR UPDATE` locks the selected rows until the transaction ends, which prevents the classic lost update where two transactions read the same balance and both write back an increment. Deadlocks happen when two transactions acquire the same two locks in opposite order; PostgreSQL detects the cycle and aborts one of them with SQLSTATE `40P01`.

data.title: A safe increment and an ordered multi-row lock
data.content: For a single counter you can avoid locking entirely with an atomic update. When you must lock several rows, always lock them in a consistent order such as ascending id.

data.title: Interview angle: deadlock prevention is ordering
data.text: You cannot eliminate deadlocks with a setting; you eliminate them with consistent lock ordering. If every transaction that touches rows A and B locks them in the same order, the circular wait is impossible. The fallback is detection and retry: catch SQLSTATE `40P01`, roll back, and retry the transaction with a short randomized backoff. Mentioning both prevention and retry is the complete answer.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: `FOR UPDATE` acquires an exclusive lock on selected rows until transaction commit.
Use `SKIP LOCKED` to build lock-free concurrent task queues.
Always access resources in a consistent global order to prevent deadlocks.
